articles.title: Launch HN: Simantic (YC F26) – Firmware Simulation for AI Agents
articles.summary:
Hi HN, we're Ahnaf and Seungmin from Simantic (https://simantic.com). We are building the simulation layer that lets engineers and AI agents test and validate firmware without hardware.
Before Simantic, we were ex-firmware engineers at companies like Neuralink and Tesla. We’ve worked on some of the coolest projects, like the Cybertruck and Roadster, back when they were still early prototypes.
We started working on firmware back when ChatGPT didn’t exist yet, but over the years, we saw how much of the engineering and development work has been automated as the frontier models improved to this point. In software, AI can run and test code inside your computer in a matter of seconds. But as firmware engineers, we didn’t have that luxury. An AI agent can write firmware in seconds, but in order to test it, we had to flash a physical board, then manually run tests using expensive and clunky tools with software made over a decade ago.
To speed up the validation loop, we built the simulation layer that lets AI agents test the firmware and make decisions based on evidence, instead of waiting for the engineer to run tests for them. We used to spend hours testing our firmware manually on devboards, but now we use our own simulation to validate firmware in seconds.
What we offer:
- Virtual devboards you can program and run with a single API call, without leaving your terminal.
- An AI code reviewer for firmware, that makes informed decisions based on evidence, using our simulation as a verification engine.
- A CI/CD pipeline for your hardware projects that validates your firmware against a simulated version of the microcontroller on every commit.
Here is a demo of our simulation used in an AI code review session: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kBK1ZjGWWbQ
Our users are using Simantic for bare-metal and RTOS development for applications like flight controllers, electric vehicles, robotics, and satellites. For safety critical systems like avionics and automotives, a robust simulation system is incredibly important, because every change in the firmware puts a human life at stake, especially for machines that cost hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars.
We recently helped an early stage space startup building satellites, to test their firmware on hardware that they don't yet have. Even the development modules for those satellites costs over $100k, and we helped them do that at just a hundredth of the cost and time.
Early on in our journey, we established our idea to make better simulation but didn’t have a clear idea of how we would do it, we considered developing our software around open source emulation frameworks like Renode (https://github.com/renode/renode) and QEMU (https://www.qemu.org/), because they were tools already used within the firmware industry. We built our MVP that was essentially a wrapper around Renode, but we quickly realized there were a lot of limitations to doing this.
1. We were bottlenecked by the development speed of Renode themselves. We tried making contributions on Github to fix issues we came across, but the speed in which we could merge our features in was not fast enough for a startup like us trying to move fast.
2. Renode is built using Dotnet, and it was proving itself to be slower than we would have liked. Renode was released in 2017, which was when all code was still being written by hand, so I think it made sense looking back, but there were limitations because of the language itself.
3. The open source tools were bloated, with features that we would never use. Yes, there were a  breadth of features, but we had a lot of things we had to work around just because we couldn’t remove or change them.
Users were complaining about simulation accuracy. Renode is an emulator at the core, but our users, especially those who are building systems where timing accuracy is crucial did not find the accuracy good enough to validate their firmware.
Because of these issues, we made our own simulation engine from scratch, fully written in Rust.
- Our simulation is focused on accuracy. Open source frameworks often focus on expandability and developer experience, which means there were a lot of tradeoffs made to prioritize a breadth of models rather than going deep into a set of select models.
- We have our own hardware validation rigs running 24/7 to ensure our simulation models are as close to real world hardware as possible, and any gaps are detected and fixed as soon as we can. It currently looks like devboards connected to a Saleae Logic MSO and a SWD bus, controlled by a Linux PC, running Claude 24/7 just finding these gaps.
Our cloud-hosted simulator is available to use right now! We also provide a native binary with our developer plan licenses that let you run your firmware on your machines locally without any limitations.
Check it out at https://simantic.com/cloud-sim, and you can start using our AI firmware reviewer bot in your own Github repos here: https://simantic.com/dashboard/simantic-bot.
We currently have support for some models of the STM32F0, F4, H7 series MCUs, ESP32-S3/C3, and RP2040, but we’re constantly working to release new models every week, and improve our existing ones.
Thank you, and if you have any questions, feel free to send us an email at founders@simantic.dev

articles.title: Custom Voices With Qwen3-TTS
articles.summary:
With my kids I’m currently building a little dungeron
crawler and we’re trying to
learn a bit about game
development along the way.
However given that we live in the modern times of increasing capabilities we
wanted to get a narrator and voice over.
But we also wanted it to not sound like everyone’s standard AI voices so I
looked into what options there are on the table.  After some investigation I
narrowed down to using Qwen3-TTS which
uses voice embeddings for custom voices.
With a bit of creativity you can also do more with those custom voices than
appears initially.  In case this is of interest to you, this post just covers
what we learned and with some examples.  You can probably point your agent to
it and it can do something with it.
What Qwen Offers
Qwen3 is not the only TTS model in town, and it wans’t even my first choice.  We
initially used Kokoro.  However
Qwen3 supports voice cloning and we wanted to have it feel a bit more unique.
In practice it’s a bit tricker though. Qwen3 ships three kinds of models:
1.7B-Base (and 0.6B): clones a voice from a few seconds of reference audio
1.7B-CustomVoice: comes with nine built-in speakers and instructions
1.7B-VoiceDesign: invents a voice from a text description
The base model clones either in context or from the speaker embedding alone but
there is no documented way to clone a voice and direct it with instructions.
That means unlike the custom voice and voice design models you cannot say “speak
sad” or “whisper” with a cloned base model.
At present the official options for a custom voice are fine-tuning Base on a
single speaker or to make a clip with VoiceDesign and clone it with Base.  That
is not all that bad, but it means instructions are gone.
Playing With It
For this blog post I took 28 seconds of me from my talk at PyAI
Conf, cut between two pauses so
that it starts and ends on a full sentence, and transcribed it with Whisper.
The transcript is really only needed for baking but to compare against an
already existing voice it’s useful to have it say the same thing as the original
recording.
Note that a conference talk recording is not ideal but it works anyways.  Which
is also a good reminder that you really don’t need a particularly clean
recording (or a very long one) to get a halfway convincing version of a person.
Particularly when then presented to you on a low quality phone call, it won’t be
very hard to trick your grandmother.
The first thing you can do is to blend that recording with another voice.  For
instance you can use VoiceDesign to make up a voice from a description.  For this blog
post the designed voice was created like this, with Qwen’s own Python package
qwen-tts (pip install qwen-tts, I used
0.1.1), which the rest of the code in this post uses too:
import torch
from qwen_tts import Qwen3TTSModel

kw = dict(device_map="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16, attn_implementation="sdpa")
design = Qwen3TTSModel.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-VoiceDesign", **kw)
wavs, sr = design.generate_voice_design(
    text=open("voices/transcript.txt").read(), language="English",
    instruct="A man in his forties with a warm, natural, medium-low voice, speaking "
             "clearly and calmly at an easy conversational pace, like someone reading "
             "aloud to a friend.",
)

You can see how the two different voices behave, particularly when blended together:
Interactive demo: see the post on the website.
Voice Embeddings
What Base takes from a recording when cloning from the embedding alone is a
speaker embedding which is basically 2048 numbers out of a speaker encoder that
was trained.  The same voice gets similar numbers and different voices get
different ones.  Which btw, is also a convenient way to do speaker detection
from recordings if you want to!  It’s not perfect, but it’s quite helpful for a
single audio track recording to tell two speakers apart if you do some basic
slicing and dicing (more on that below).
Because it is just a vector, you can do arithmetic on it.  For instance a
weighted average of two embeddings is a spaker that is somewhere between two
voices:
base = Qwen3TTSModel.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base", **kw)

def fingerprint(path):
    prompt = base.create_voice_clone_prompt(ref_audio=path, x_vector_only_mode=True)
    return prompt[0].ref_spk_embedding

def blend(a, b, t):
    a, b = a.float(), b.float()
    mixed = (1 - t) * a + t * b
    return (mixed / mixed.norm() * ((1 - t) * a.norm() + t * b.norm())).to(torch.bfloat16)

armin, designed = fingerprint("voices/armin.flac"), fingerprint("voices/designed.flac")

Here is the same sentence in eleven blends:
Interactive demo: see the post on the website.
Note that it stops sounding like me quite quickly, but it retains some of my
features.  And it for sure ends up with creating a unique voice regardless.
I found some better successes when ensuing that the two voices have similar
spectograms (eg: similar “recording setups”).  In this recording you can hear
that one voice picked up by the lapel mic was a bit hollow compared to the
designed voice.
If you like a a voice that comes out, you can bake it back into a new recording
that you can then use as reference:
import soundfile as sf

mixed = blend(armin, designed, 0.5)
audio, rate = say(open("voices/transcript.txt").read(), mixed)  # say() is shown further down
sf.write("voices/final.flac", audio, rate)
final = fingerprint("voices/final.flac")

The baked voice does not come back exactly as the blend but it makes handling it
easier if you want to.  It’s just one voice reference file.
So on the question of using those embeddings for speaker recognition: how good
does that work?  I took an episode of State of Agentic
Coding, the podcast Ben and I
record, cut it into 2-second windows one second apart and compared each with an
embedding of me form the conference.
Somewhat surprising, but maybe not too surprising using my conference recording
clip as the reference this does not work at all with Qwen3.  If instead I take
the 20 seconds where I introduce myself at the start of the episode as the
reference, it gets 98% of the rest right. 
On the other hand using a model that was trained for speaker verification
instead does manage to pick me up from the conference recording clip.  For
instance ECAPA,
finds me from the conference clip in 97% of the windows.
Here are 20 minutes of that podcast, classified by speaker with the different
approaches:
Interactive demo: see the post on the website.
Instructed Cloned Voices
But the embeddings a very useful for the voice cloning!  But how to give them
instructions?  Base and CustomVoice manipulate the speaker the same way: one
vector inserted into the talker’s input sequence.  In CustomVoice that vector is
a row of the embedding table.  In Base it is the x-vector from the speaker
encoder, which only Base has.  The generation code takes either
(voice_clone_prompt is a regular argument of generate), and the transformer
weights of the two models are nearly identical.  So take the embedding with
Base, then hand it to CustomVoice instead of one of its speakers:
cv = Qwen3TTSModel.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-CustomVoice", **kw)

def say(text, xvec, instruct=None, language="English"):
    ids = cv._tokenize_texts([cv._build_assistant_text(text)])
    told = [cv._tokenize_texts([cv._build_instruct_text(instruct)])[0]
            if instruct else None]
    voice = {"ref_code": [None], "ref_spk_embedding": [xvec],
             "x_vector_only_mode": [True], "icl_mode": [False]}
    codes, _ = cv.model.generate(
        input_ids=ids, instruct_ids=told, voice_clone_prompt=voice,
        languages=[language], non_streaming_mode=True,
        **cv._merge_generate_kwargs(temperature=0.7, subtalker_temperature=0.7),
    )
    wavs, rate = cv.model.speech_tokenizer.decode([{"audio_codes": codes[0]}])
    return wavs[0], rate

wav, rate = say("I really thought this would work.", armin,
                "Speak in a sad, sorrowful tone, voice low and heavy, on the verge of tears.")

Pick a speaker for the slot, a model and an instruction:
Interactive demo: see the post on the website.
Instructions work on cloned voices, but less reliably than on the built-in
speakers, and it depends on the emotion, but honestly, it came out better than I
anticipated.  Definitely good enough to have some true custom voices for a voice
over that don’t necessarily sound like something, someone else has in their
game.
Other Fun Math
If a voice is a point in a 2048-dimensional space and blending works we can maybe
do some other funny math on it.  The obvious one is to try to see if some math can
be used to manipulate gender.
To find it I had VoiceDesign create 14 different voices for men and women each.
When you then take the average woman minus the average man you can then move any
voice along that direction:
women = torch.stack([fingerprint(f"design/f{i}.wav") for i in range(14)]).float()
men = torch.stack([fingerprint(f"design/m{i}.wav") for i in range(14)]).float()
middle = (women.mean(0) + men.mean(0)) / 2
axis = women.mean(0) - men.mean(0)
axis = axis / axis.norm()

def move(xvec, t):
    """Put the voice at position t along the gender axis, keep the rest."""
    x = xvec.float()
    return (x + (t - (x - middle) @ axis) * axis).to(torch.bfloat16)

Here is the result for my clone:
Interactive demo: see the post on the website.
Anyways, that’s that.  If you want to play around with Qwen3 TTS I hope this was
of some help, and maybe you got some ideas of what to do with the voice
embeddings.  Use it for good, not evil.

articles.title: Show HN: Overtone – Transcribe, correct and cut captions for any screen shape
articles.summary:
Hi HN, I'm Ruud, co-founder of Lont. We turn company emails into personalized videos.
Video captions cost us manual work twice: fixing misheard words, then fixing layout, like lines ending on “the”.
Overtone uses multiple models to listen to the audio: gpt-transcribe, Azure STT, and Elevenlabs Scribe. When they return conflicting results, Overtone sends small clips to the models again, and then lets an LLM decide what was actually said.
The LLM is like a human doing a sanity check on the transcription model. Humans would easily recognize a word to be different based on context. The LLM basically does the same, using an optional context prompt + its world knowledge. Because of this the Word Error Rate (WER) on many test files is lower when using Overtone, compared to just using a model without it.
Sure, the cost is higher because we use up to 3 different STT models + an LLM, but it still removes mistakes, reducing the time needed to fix captions to a minimum, and reducing the chance you'll miss something. For us it's worth it. For ultra high volume use cases it may not be.
The rules-based cutter nicely cuts the transcript into captions that look good, depending on screen size: 16:9 is different from 9:16, and the Overtone Format we created supports any type really. Pauses become breaks, captions are grouped per speaker, and names/numbers are never spread out over multiple captions.
How to add these captions to your videos? A videojs plugin can do this automatically, so you don't burn in your captions. The plugin lets you cycle between styled captions, plain captions, and off. You can burn them into an MP4 file with overtone burn.
Quickly try it out just the cutter? Try:
  npx overtone-captions recut yoursub.srt

We open-sourced this first version (MIT) because we believe many people can benefit from this, especially if your captions just need to be good. There's plenty of room to improve though, so we've made it easy to help contribute to add style packs, languages, and providers/models.
You can find a demo at: https://overtone.lont.ai/
Find the code and benchmarks here: https://github.com/lonthq/overtone-captions

articles.title: Rolfe Winkler at The WSJ: ‘The Beleaguered Chip Sellers Getting Their Revenge on Apple’
articles.summary:
Rolfe Winkler, in a crackerjack story for The Wall Street Journal (gift link):
Blevins, who left Apple in 2022, sometimes set up
back-to-back meetings with suppliers so that rival sales teams
might run into each other, stoking competitive tension. Sales
representatives learned to pack nutrition bars to sustain them
through negotiating sessions that Apple executives sometimes
pushed past midnight without a dinner break. Blevins’s bad-cop
reputation gave his staff leverage: They threatened to call him in
if contract terms weren’t to their liking.
One significant contract term allowed Apple to audit its
suppliers’ books. Flash makers typically had to designate Apple
as a “most favored customer,” which guaranteed that no other
buyer got a lower price, according to people familiar with the
agreements. Apple’s audits allowed it to verify that no one
paid less.
Apple caught Micron selling flash at cheaper prices to another
customer and won an arbitration settlement worth tens of millions
of dollars more than a decade ago, said people familiar with the
dispute. Apple audited its suppliers so often that Blevins
negotiated a volume discount with the auditor, Deloitte.
The whole story is a fascinating and entertaining read. But I don’t get the “revenge” angle in the headline. The biggest buyers can negotiate the best deals. Apple used to be the biggest buyer, by far, for flash memory chips. They negotiated, with hardball but above-the-board tactics, the best deals. Now, Apple isn’t the biggest buyer — the AI datacenter hyperscalers are. Apple no longer gets the best deals. But they’re still getting fair deals. Apple is still negotiating the best deals it can for itself. So where is the “revenge”? The pinch mostly isn’t being felt by Apple — it’s being felt by Apple’s customers, who now face significantly higher product prices.
I included “mostly” in the preceding sentence because Winkler, in collaboration with the research firm TechInsights, makes the case in the piece that the rising costs of flash memory have eaten into the remarkably juicy profit margins Apple has historically earned from higher-storage upgrades.
What I also don’t get, at all, is the participation in the story by Scott Nelson, the chief marketing officer at Kioxia (which I learned in this story is the new name for the company formerly known as Toshiba Memory Corporation), a major flash supplier. Nelson told Winkler he so loathes Apple that he shot his old iPod with a rifle and keeps the pieces on his desk. The article ends thus:
The industry’s low point came in 2023. The Covid-era,
work-from-home device boom cooled, and flash prices bottomed out
at 5 cents a gigabyte. Bernstein Research estimated the flash
industry generated operating losses of $19 billion that year,
while Apple earned $14 billion in gross profit selling extra flash
storage.
Those were tough times that “I hope we don’t ever see again,” said
Nelson, the Kioxia sales executive.
Yes, I’m sure the current AI datacenter mania will last forever, the bubble will never burst, and that even if it does, that no one at Apple will remember Nelson’s participation in this story.
 ★

This turnaround is a big deal to Apple fans. Ternus shrugs off the
drama. “The Mac is first and foremost an indirect input device,
built around the trackpad and keyboard. But I think there’s times
when it’s comfortable and handy to have touch.”
Ternus and Apple want to make sure that the Mac faithful don’t
panic that the 42-year-old franchise is losing its identity to
Apple’s gangbusters mobile products. “We needed to get to a point
where adding touch didn’t make the product lesser in any way. It
didn’t make it heavier. It didn’t make it thicker. That came
together with the OLED screen, the best display we’ve ever put
into a Mac,” Ternus told me. “All of these things, and, oh yeah,
it has touch as well.”
After a long fun day of hands-on exploration, briefings, and a slew of demos, not just most, but all of my concerns about touchscreen support adversely affecting the Mac UI have been allayed. I love it. These seem like exquisite machines even if you never want to touch the screen. I think what Ternus told Levy captures the truth of touch’s role: “All of these things, and, oh yeah, it has touch as well.”

articles.title: Extremely brief history of PDP computers
articles.summary:
I don’t know why I started to put this together. These machines fascinate me,
because so much of early computing/hacker type culture happened on them. I
started writing a table, but realised a timeline would be more intuitive. In
this graph, the price is for a minimal configuration and adjusted for inflation.
The time is the memory cycle time, a decent proxy for speed.













Some notes:





The PDP-1 was created mostly as an experiment. At the time, industrial
control systems used either humans or complicated contraptions of logic boards
to make decisions. Some engineers at DEC wanted to see if there was a
customer base willing to use general-purpose computers instead.
The PDP-4 was a variant of PDP-1 that was a little slower and much
cheaper. It was not compatible with the PDP-1. The PDP-4 was upgraded with
new chip technology and became the PDP-7, which was then optimised further
for cost and speed and became the PDP-9.
The PDP-5 was created when they realised the PDP-1 and PDP-4 machines
were overkill for industrial control systems. By being smaller, it could be
much cheaper, at the cost of compatibility with PDP-1 and PDP-4. It was
still intended for roughly the same market. The chip upgrade turned it into
the PDP-8.
The PDP-6 was a completely different beast, aimed at a different market. It
supported having tonnes of directly-addressable memory, as well as memory
protection, so it could be used as a time-sharing system. The amount of memory
made it run Lisp well. With the chip upgrade, it became the PDP-10.
The PDP-11 was a new architecture again, intended to subsume all the
previous models, to avoid running three incompatible lines in parallel. There
were many variants of the PDP-11, with various performance characteristics
and corresponding price points. However, even its most powerful configuration
wasn’t powerful enough to attract many PDP-10 users.
The VAX came much later, but it’s included in the table anyway because it is
what eventually subsumed the PDP-10. The VAX was somewhat compatible with
the PDP-11, but they served different markets.
(Continue reading the full article on the web.)

articles.title: Celebrating SIM Cards
articles.summary:
It’s time to celebrate a little win.
The other day, my mom contacted me saying her 10-year-old iPhone wouldn’t turn on.
After getting a hold of the device and doing some family IT support, I concluded the battery was dead.
So I bought her a new (old) one on Walmart (SE 3rd gen., if you must know).
Her old phone used a SIM card, so I was expecting the process to go something like this:
Take the SIM out of the old phone
Put it in the new phone
Setup the device
Troubleshoot why there was no service
Call my Mom’s carrier and work through the issue
But step 4 and 5 never happened.
The new phone “just” connected. I called her number. I texted it. Everything worked as expected.
Everything worked as expected.
Everything worked as expected.
I didn’t have to Google a single question.
I was floored.
Flabbergasted.
I know I shouldn’t have been because that’s how SIM cards are supposed to work, right? Like that’s the whole promise of a SIM card: you can seamlessly swap them between phones.
And in this case, the tech worked exactly as promised.
As I write this, I’m kind of amazed at how amazed I am that everything “just worked”.
Shout out to anyone who has ever worked on SIM card technology.
More things like this please :)
Email
      · Mastodon ·

      Bluesky
